title: How many halves fit in three?
objectives: Divide by a fraction by counting how many times it fits
Explain why dividing by a fraction is multiplying by it upside down
Handle a division that does not come out whole

screens.prose: You have 3 chocolate bars, laid end to end on this line. Each friend who visits gets half a bar.
screens.question: How many friends can you feed?

hints.text: How many halves are in one bar?
Each bar gives 2 halves. Three bars give 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the half-bar portions along the line.

byKey.halved: You found half of 3 bars. The question asks how many half bars fit into 3.
byKey.bars: You gave each friend a whole bar. Half a bar each feeds twice as many.

explain.text: Each bar holds 2 halves, so 3 bars hold 6. You counted how many halves fit into 3. Keep that question in mind: how many fit?

screens.prose: Now a portion is $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of a bar. You have 2 bars, end to end. Each mark on the line is a third of a bar.
screens.question: Drag the point to where 3 portions end, starting from 0.

hints.text: How many marks does one portion cover?
One portion ends 2 marks along from 0.
Each portion is 2 thirds. Three portions are 6 thirds, which is 2 whole bars.

feedback.correct: Three portions of two thirds end exactly at 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Step 2 marks for each portion, three times.

byKey.one: You marked one portion. Keep going: 3 portions, each 2 thirds.
byKey.thirds: You marked 3 thirds. Each portion is 2 thirds, so 3 portions are 6 thirds.

explain.text: Three portions of $\tfrac{2}{3}$ end exactly at 2. So exactly 3 portions fit into 2 bars, with nothing left over.

screens.prose: Asking how many portions fit is **dividing**. You found $2 \div \tfrac{2}{3} = 3$: three portions of two thirds fit into 2. Each mark on this line is a quarter.
screens.question: What is $3 \div \tfrac{3}{4}$?

hints.text: How many quarter marks are in 3 bars?
One portion of $\tfrac{3}{4}$, the arrow, covers 3 quarter marks.
Three bars hold 12 quarters. Each portion uses 3, so 4 portions fit.

feedback.correct: Four portions of three quarters fit into 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many three-quarter portions fit along the line.

byKey.times: You took $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of 3. The question asks how many three-quarter portions fit into 3.
byKey.upside: You worked out $\tfrac{3}{4} \div 3$, the other way round. Count how many three quarters fit into 3.

explain.text: Three bars hold 12 quarters, and each portion takes 3 of them. So 4 portions fit: $3 \div \tfrac{3}{4} = 4$. Dividing by a fraction less than one gave more than we started with.

screens.prose: Some divisions do not come out whole. You have 1 bar, and a portion is still $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of a bar. Each mark is a third.
screens.question: How many portions of $\tfrac{2}{3}$ fit into 1 bar? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: One portion fits. What is left over?
The arrow is one portion: 2 marks of the 3 in the bar.
After one portion, 1 third is left. That is half of a 2-third portion, so one and a half portions fit.

feedback.correct: One portion and half of another.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. After one portion, compare the leftover with a whole portion.

byKey.whole-only: You counted only full portions. The third left over is half a portion, and it counts.
byKey.times: You took $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of 1. The question asks how many portions fit.
byKey.left: You counted the leftover as a third of a portion. It is 1 third of a bar, which is half of a 2-third portion.

explain.text: One portion fits with a third of a bar left over. That third is half a portion, so $1 \div \tfrac{2}{3} = 1\tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{3}{2}$. Notice the answer is $\tfrac{2}{3}$ turned upside down.

screens.prose: Dividing a fraction by a fraction works the same way. The bar shows $\tfrac{3}{4}$, and each mark is an eighth.
screens.question: What is $\tfrac{3}{4} \div \tfrac{1}{8}$?

widget.label: Three quarters divided by one eighth

hints.text: How many eighths make a quarter?
The bar is $\tfrac{3}{4}$. Count the eighth steps under it.
Each quarter is 2 eighths. Three quarters are 6 eighths.

feedback.correct: Six eighths fit under three quarters.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the eighths under the bar.

byKey.times: You took $\tfrac{1}{8}$ of $\tfrac{3}{4}$. Count how many eighths fit inside $\tfrac{3}{4}$.
byKey.quarters: You counted quarters. The portions here are eighths, half the size, so twice as many fit.

explain.text: You counted 6 eighths under $\tfrac{3}{4}$. Renaming $\tfrac{3}{4}$ as $\tfrac{6}{8}$ makes the count plain. With the same piece size, dividing is counting.

screens.prose: Sam works out $6 \div \tfrac{1}{2}$ and gets 3. He says dividing always makes a number smaller. Each mark on this line is a half.
screens.question: What is $6 \div \tfrac{1}{2}$?

options.why: You halved 6. Dividing by 2 shares 6 into 2 parts; dividing by $\tfrac{1}{2}$ counts the halves in 6.
You divided the half by 6, the other way round. Count how many halves fit into 6.

hints.text: How many halves are in one whole?
Six wholes hold 2 halves each: 12 in all.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the half steps from 0 to 6.

byKey.halved: You divided by 2, which shares 6 into 2 parts. Dividing by $\tfrac{1}{2}$ asks how many halves fit into 6.

explain.text: Each of the 6 wholes holds 2 halves, so 12 halves fit. Dividing by 2 and dividing by $\tfrac{1}{2}$ are different questions. Dividing by a fraction less than one gives a bigger number.

screens.prose: Look back. One whole holds 2 halves, 8 eighths, or $\tfrac{3}{2}$ portions of $\tfrac{2}{3}$. Each time, that is the fraction turned upside down. So dividing by a fraction is multiplying by it upside down: $$2 \div \frac{2}{3} = 2 \times \frac{3}{2} = 3$$
screens.question: What is $4 \div \tfrac{2}{5}$?

options.why: You multiplied by $\tfrac{2}{5}$ without turning it over. That finds $\tfrac{2}{5}$ of 4, not how many fit.
You turned the whole question round, finding $\tfrac{2}{5} \div 4$. Turn over only the fraction you divide by.
You divided 4 by 2 and ignored the fifths. Each portion is 2 fifths, much smaller than 2.

hints.text: How many portions of $\tfrac{2}{5}$ fit into one whole?
One whole holds $\tfrac{5}{2}$ portions. Four wholes hold $4 \times \tfrac{5}{2} = 10$.

feedback.correct: Four times five halves is ten.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn $\tfrac{2}{5}$ upside down and multiply.

explain.text: One whole holds 5 fifths, which is $\tfrac{5}{2}$ portions of 2 fifths. Four wholes hold 4 times as many: $4 \times \tfrac{5}{2} = 10$.

screens.prose: Put the lines in order to show why dividing by $\tfrac{2}{3}$ is the same as multiplying by $\tfrac{3}{2}$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: A portion is 2 thirds, so one bar holds $\tfrac{3}{2}$ portions.
Two bars hold twice as many: $2 \times \tfrac{3}{2}$ portions.

hints.text: Start from what one bar is made of.
The upside-down fraction appears when we count portions in one bar.
Thirds in a bar, portions in a bar, portions in two bars, conclude.

feedback.correct: Thirds, portions in one bar, portions in two bars, conclude.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line uses a count from the line before it.

byKey.one-bar: Portions in a bar come from the thirds in a bar. Start with the thirds.
byKey.two-bars: You doubled before finding what one bar holds. Count portions in one bar first.

explain.text: One bar holds 3 thirds, which is $\tfrac{3}{2}$ portions of 2 thirds. Two bars hold twice that. The upside-down fraction is the number of portions in one whole.

screens.prose: Markets quote prices in steps called **ticks**. In this market a tick is $\tfrac{1}{8}$ of a pound. A share price rises by $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of a pound in one day.
screens.question: How many ticks did the price rise?

hints.text: How many eighths of a pound are in a quarter of a pound?
The bar shows the rise; each mark is one tick.
$\tfrac{3}{4} \div \tfrac{1}{8} = \tfrac{3}{4} \times 8 = 6$.

feedback.correct: Six ticks of an eighth of a pound.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many ticks fit into the rise.

byKey.times: You took $\tfrac{1}{8}$ of $\tfrac{3}{4}$. Count how many eighths fit into the rise.
byKey.upside: You divided the tick by the rise. Count ticks inside the rise: the rise divided by the tick.
byKey.quarters: You counted quarters of a pound. A tick is an eighth, so twice as many fit.

explain.text: The rise of $\tfrac{3}{4}$ is $\tfrac{6}{8}$ of a pound, so 6 ticks fit. As a division, $\tfrac{3}{4} \div \tfrac{1}{8} = \tfrac{3}{4} \times 8 = 6$. A trader would say the price moved 6 ticks.

ideas: Dividing by a fraction asks how many of it fit. $3 \div \tfrac{1}{2}$ counts the halves in 3.
One whole holds the fraction turned upside down: $\tfrac{3}{2}$ portions of $\tfrac{2}{3}$. So divide by turning over and multiplying.
Dividing by a fraction less than one gives a bigger number, and a leftover counts as part of a portion.

formula.name: Dividing by a fraction
formula.note: Turn over only the fraction you divide by: $2 \div \tfrac{2}{3} = 2 \times \tfrac{3}{2} = 3$.

summary.trap: Dividing by $\tfrac{1}{2}$ is not dividing by 2. $6 \div \tfrac{1}{2} = 12$, but $6 \div 2 = 3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many thirds fit into 4.

byKey.times: You took a third of 4. Count how many thirds fit into 4.
byKey.upside: You divided the third by 4. Turn over only the fraction you divide by.

explain.text: Each whole holds 3 thirds, so 4 wholes hold 12. In the rule, $4 \div \tfrac{1}{3} = 4 \times 3 = 12$.

options.why: You multiplied the fractions. Count how many quarters fit into three quarters.
You found what part of $\tfrac{3}{4}$ one quarter is. The question asks how many quarters fit.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count quarters inside three quarters.

explain.text: Both amounts are in quarters, so we count: 3 quarters hold 3 portions of 1 quarter.

widget.label: A half divided by a quarter

feedback.correct: Two quarters fit into a half.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many quarters fit into a half.

byKey.times: You took a quarter of a half. Count how many quarters fit into a half.
byKey.upside: You divided the quarter by the half, the other way round. Ask how many quarters fit into a half.

explain.text: A half is 2 quarters, so 2 quarters fit. The rule agrees: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 4 = 2$.

options.why: You expected multiplying to give more. Multiplying by a half halves 5; dividing by a half doubles it.
You treated dividing and multiplying by a half as the same. One gives 10, the other $2\tfrac{1}{2}$.

feedback.correct: Ten against two and a half.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out each one.

explain.text: Ten halves fit into 5, so $5 \div \tfrac{1}{2} = 10$. Half of 5 is $5 \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 2\tfrac{1}{2}$.
